name: A Surround That Describes A Wall That Is Not There
aka: quoined surround on a frame wall
the flush window in a mass wall
symptom: Two opposite versions of one error. Either a heavy masonry surround — quoined jambs, moulded architrave, keystone — is applied to a wall that has no thickness to justify it, most often a thin stucco or veneer skin over a frame, where the canonical treatment for the style is no surround at all. Or a wall that is meant to express mass has its windows set flush at the outer face, with a reveal of an inch or less, so the opening reads as a hole cut in paper.

cause.explanation: Both versions come from the same substitution: the wall was not built the way the language assumes, and the opening is where the substitution becomes visible. A 2 in stucco skin over a frame cannot produce a 10 in reveal, so the window goes at the face where the flashing is easiest and the framing is shallowest. Conversely, a facade with no thickness at all is given catalogue surrounds to supply the gravity the wall lacks. Deep reveals also cost real money in a frame wall — furred jambs, sloped sills, additional flashing at every return.
cause.cost_saved: A flush window in a stucco skin saves 150 to 400 USD an opening against a returned or splayed reveal; on twenty openings, 3,000 to 8,000 USD. Applied surrounds are the cheaper way to buy apparent weight.

rule_violated.statement: Window reveal depth not less than 8 in. A flush window in a stucco wall destroys the expression of mass on which the entire idiom depends, and is the single most common failure in contemporary versions.
Minimum 6 in reveal, jambs returned or splayed in stucco with no applied wood casing. Flush windows in a thin stucco skin void the style.
Minimum 6 in reveal, often 12 to 18 in, so every window sits in a visible shadow box; this single measurement separates a real example from a stucco-clad frame house at fifty feet.
A door in a hole. The entrance is the one place a Georgian house always spends money, even the plainest.
Ornament essentially absent: no shutters, no keystones, no applied classical elements. The canonical surround is a flat board.

correct_practice: Ask what the wall is, and let the opening report it truthfully. A mass or mass-expressing wall gets its shadow from depth: reveal 6 in minimum in Mediterranean and Spanish Colonial Revival, 8 in minimum in Andalusian, 10 in in Pueblo Revival, 12 to 24 in in Richardsonian Romanesque, 12 in in Beaux-Arts, achieved by returning or splaying the jamb in the wall material with no applied wood casing. A thin-skinned frame wall gets its shadow from applied trim, and that trim should be flat and broad rather than sculptural, because a moulded stone-derived profile in a nailed board is a lie the material will not carry. Styles whose canonical surround is none — Shingle Style, Prairie, Modern Farmhouse, Mission Revival, Pueblo Revival — get nothing, and a surround added to them is not an enrichment but a category error.

fixes.right: Build the reveal. In a frame wall pretending to mass, this means furring the exterior out 4 to 6 in with continuous exterior insulation, which the energy code increasingly wants anyway, and setting the window at the inner face. The insulation pays for the reveal.
fixes.cheap: Set the window at the inner face of the framing rather than at the sheathing, and return the stucco or the head and jamb into the opening. In a 2x6 wall with sheathing and a stucco assembly this yields a 6 1/2 to 7 in reveal at no material cost whatever — the same window, the same wall, a different position within it. This is the highest-value zero-cost move available on a Mediterranean or Spanish elevation.
fixes.dishonest: An applied foam surround with a stucco skin, sometimes moulded as a splayed reveal, glued to the face of the wall around a flush window. The shadow it casts is on the wrong side and at the wrong scale, and it becomes obvious the first time the sun is low, because a real reveal darkens the whole opening while an applied band darkens only itself.

detection: For the mass-wall case, find the shadow inside the opening. At midday a 6 in reveal puts the whole head and one jamb in hard shade and the window glass reads as a dark rectangle set back; a flush window reads as a bright rectangle in the same plane as the wall. Measure the shadow band at the head as a fraction of the opening width — under 0.03 means no reveal. For the applied-surround case, look at the return: an applied surround stops at the corner of the wall or dies into siding, and its ends are cut square; a real masonry surround turns the corner or terminates on a real quoin. Also check whether the surround's material appears anywhere else on the building; a single-purpose material used only around windows is a catalogue accessory.

exceptions.why: The style's canonical answer is no surround and near-zero casing, and adding one is the fault in the opposite direction.
exceptions.bounds: Casing 3 in maximum, projection 1 in maximum, no projecting hoods or moulded sills.

bounds_test.note: Casing 3 in maximum, projection 1 in maximum.

exceptions.why: Flat, broad, unmoulded surrounds on a frame wall are correct and are the style's method; the flatness is a positive statement about board construction rather than an imitation of stone.
exceptions.bounds: Broad and flat. The moment a Greek Revival surround acquires a keystone or a moulded architrave it has left the style.

bounds_test.note: Broad and flat. The moment a Greek Revival surround acquires a keystone or a moulded architrave it has left the style; the flatness is the licence and the depth is not.

applies_when.note: The flat surround is a statement about board construction; on a masonry Greek Revival the reveal rules return.

exceptions.why: The style requires masonry or stucco walls to express thickness with a minimum 5 in reveal, quoins, water table or a returned surround, so a substantial surround is not applique but the wall reporting itself.
exceptions.bounds: The wall must actually be masonry or must carry the 5 in reveal. Flush-set windows in a thin veneer wall break the style by its own constraint.

bounds_test.note: The style's own minimum. Flush-set windows in a thin veneer wall break the style by its own constraint, so the exception is self-limiting.

applies_when.note: Depends on the wall being masonry or stucco expressing thickness, not on the style label.

exceptions.why: Elaborated stone surrounds with voussoirs, keystones and rustication are the style's proper vocabulary.
exceptions.bounds: The wall must be, or must fully express, cut stone: minimum 12 in reveal, jambs returned in the face material, true voussoirs, rusticated base of not less than one storey.

bounds_test.note: Minimum 12 in reveal, jambs returned in the face material, true voussoirs, rusticated base of not less than one storey.

confused_with.difference: That fault is a single applique member on a head. This is the whole surround misdescribing the wall it sits in, and it includes the opposite case of no surround where depth was required.
That fault is about a correctly conceived casing being too narrow. This is about the surround belonging to a different construction altogether.

sources: NPS Preservation Brief 22, the preservation and repair of historic stucco

test.note: CONDITIONAL: applies where the wall is or claims to be mass. Read from the shadow — at midday a 6 in reveal puts the whole head and one jamb in hard shade and the glass reads as a dark rectangle set back, while a flush window reads as a bright rectangle in the wall plane. Style floors: Spanish Colonial Revival and Mediterranean 6 in, French Eclectic 5 in, Andalusian 8 in, Pueblo 10 in, Beaux-Arts 12 in, Richardsonian 12 to 24 in.

secondary_tests.note: The scale-free version, which works without knowing the opening size: the shadow at the head as a fraction of the opening width. Under 0.03 there is effectively no reveal.

THE APPLIQUE TEST, running the other way. A single-purpose material used only around windows is a catalogue accessory. A real masonry surround shares its material with a water table, a quoin, a belt course or a base; a cast surround appears nowhere else and dies into siding with a square-cut end.

severity_by_style.why: The style names it: a flush window in a stucco wall destroys the expression of mass on which the entire idiom depends, and is the single most common failure in contemporary versions.
Flush windows in a thin stucco skin void the style by its own constraint.
The reveal is the single measurement that separates a real example from a stucco-clad frame house at fifty feet.
The style is entirely a wall style and thin stone veneer over frame is prohibited outright.
The canonical answer is no surround and near-zero casing; the fault here runs in the opposite direction.
Flat broad surrounds on a frame wall are correct and are a positive statement about board construction rather than an imitation of stone.

inverted_by.statement: A surround is the fault. Casing 3 in maximum, projection 1 in maximum, no projecting hoods or moulded sills.
An applied classical surround is the fault: the style node states that ornament is essentially absent — no keystones, no applied classical elements.
A carved or cast entrance or window surround is the fault, and its presence reclassifies the building as Spanish Colonial Revival.
Any applied surround is the fault; the opening is bounded by continuous bands.
An applied surround is the fault, and so is a shallow reveal — the two errors are simultaneous and opposite, which is what makes this idiom the hardest to fake.
